unit.title: Business quality and macro
unit.description: Competitive advantages, the cycle, interest rates, macro data and how to analyse a company

texts: Moat or not?
Why do you stay on WhatsApp even when a better app comes out? Because your friends are there: that's a **moat**, as Buffett calls it, an advantage the competition can't copy.
Moat
Not a moat
A patented drug
Intangible: nobody can copy it for years.
A social network with billions of users
Network effect: every user makes it more useful for everyone else.
A good TV advert
Any competitor can pay for one.
The management software a whole company runs on
Switching costs: changing it takes lots of time and money.
A distributor that buys more cheaply than anyone
Cost advantage: it sells cheap and still makes money.
This summer's must-have product
Fads pass; a moat lasts.
The only oil pipeline in a region
Efficient scale: the market only has room for one.
Sort the seven advantages.
A **moat** is an advantage that's **hard to copy** and lasts: intangibles, switching costs, network effects, cost advantage or efficient scale.
Ask yourself: could a competitor with money copy it tomorrow?
Is it hard to copy?
2000: the best business in the world
Uncle Luis
The year 2000. Microsoft is one of the best companies in the world.
Everyone uses Windows. I'm buying shares, whatever the price.
Careful: Microsoft and Cisco trade on P/Es of between 60 and 100.
What do you tell Uncle Luis?
With a business like that, the price doesn't matter
Anyone who bought at the 2000 peak took about **16 years** to get back to it.
Great business, but check whether the price is reasonable
Exactly. The business stayed excellent; the problem was the price.
Wait until they recommend it on TV
Better to check the price yourself. When everyone's talking about something, it's usually expensive.
Oh dear. Good business… and a bad buy.
A good business needs a moat. A good investment also needs a good price.

steps.title: How a moat shows up in the numbers
steps.body:
• **High, stable** margins and ROIC for 10 years.
• It can **raise prices** without losing customers, even with inflation.
• It holds on to or gains **market share**.
steps.key: A good business needs a moat; a good investment also needs a good price.
steps.tip: Try it: ask Lumi what moat an app you use every day has.

texts: Cyclical or defensive?
If you lost your job tomorrow, you'd keep buying food but put off the summer trip. Companies go through the same thing in a crisis: sort each business.
Cyclical
Defensive
Carmaker
A new car gets put off when times get tough.
Supermarket
People keep buying food in any crisis.
Airline
Travel is one of the first things to get cut.
Electricity company
People pay the electricity bill, crisis or not.
Luxury brand
Pricey treats get put off.
Drugmaker
Nobody stops taking medicine because of a recession.
Construction company
Very sensitive to jobs, credit and interest rates.
Bank
In a recession, defaults rise and less gets lent.
Sort the eight businesses.
What people buy just the same in a crisis is **defensive**: it falls less and rises less. What gets put off is **cyclical**: it rises more in expansions and falls more in recessions.
Ask yourself: would I stop buying this if I lost my job?
Sort each business
March 2020
January 2020. You invest **€10,000** in the Nasdaq 100, the index of the big tech companies. A pandemic arrives and the economy stops. Real data, day by day.
In March 2020 the headlines are all about recession and record unemployment. When do you think the stock market hit bottom?
When the economic data improved
While the news was still terrible
It didn't recover all year
It bottomed out on **20 March 2020**, 28 % below its February high, when the news was still terrible.
Make it to the end, whether you sell or not.
The stock market **looks ahead**: it looks at what it expects 6 or 12 months out. In 2020, the Nasdaq 100 bottomed out on 20 March and by early June it had already regained its high.
You've sold. Watch what happens next…
Down more than 20 % in weeks. The headlines are scary. Can you hold on?
Hit «Start». You can sell whenever you like

steps.title: The economic cycle
steps.body:
1. **Recovery:** low interest rates, the economy starts to grow.
2. **Expansion:** high employment and rising profits; inflation may appear.
3. **Slowdown:** rates go up and growth slows.
4. **Recession:** GDP falls (technically, two quarters in a row) and unemployment rises.

The stock market usually falls **before** a recession and rises **before** it ends: in March 2009 and March 2020 it hit bottom amid terrible news.
steps.key: The stock market doesn't look at the present: it looks at what it expects 6 or 12 months ahead.
steps.tip: Try it: in Market, check the sector of Inditex and of Iberdrola: which is defensive?

texts: The ECB raises rates
Dani
The ECB wants inflation close to **2 %** over the medium term. Right now it's quite a bit higher.
The news says the ECB is raising rates. How does that affect me?
Dani has a variable-rate mortgage and a savings deposit. What happens to him?
He pays more on the mortgage and earns more on the deposit
That's it. Money gets dearer for borrowers and pays savers more.
Nothing: that only affects banks
Interest rates are the **price of money**: they affect almost everything.
Only his mortgage goes up
And his deposit will also pay a bit more.
With dearer loans, people spend and invest less. The economy cools.
And inflation falls, but with a **12-24 month** lag.
And the stock market?
Future profits are worth less today. And deposits and bonds compete with it.
Your mortgage when rates go up
A variable-rate mortgage of **€150,000** over 25 years. Today you pay **2 %**. The central bank raises rates and your mortgage is reviewed…
If your rate goes from 2 % to 4 %, how much does the monthly payment go up?
About €15
About €155
It doubles
It goes from **€635.78** to **€791.76**: €156 more every month, almost €1,900 a year.
Raise the rate to 4 % and look at the payment.
Interest rates are the **price of money**: when they rise, families with variable-rate mortgages have less to spend, and indebted companies have less to invest. That's how the economy cools down.
At 5 %, almost €880 a month: €240 more than at the start.
If rates fall, the opposite happens: the payment drops and there's more left to spend.
Raise the interest rate and look at the payment
Who suffers most?
Interest rates go up. Who feels it most?
Suffers more
Suffers less
Young tech company with no profits
Its value lies in distant profits, which get discounted more.
Bank
At first it earns more on its loans. If the economy slows sharply, it suffers too.
Heavily indebted company
The interest it pays goes up.
A new savings deposit
It will pay more interest than before.
Property company
It lives on debt and mortgages: everything gets dearer.
30-year bond
The longer it is, the more its price falls.
Debt-free supermarket
People keep buying food and it pays no interest.
Sort all seven.
When money gets dearer, **the future is worth less**. In 2022, the fastest rate rises in decades sent the Nasdaq down more than 30 % and long-dated bonds down more than 20 %.
Does it depend on distant profits or on debt?
Sort each one

steps.title: The price of money
steps.body:
• **ECB:** inflation target of **2 %** over the medium term.
• **Federal Reserve:** stable prices and maximum employment.

The ECB's benchmark rate is the **deposit facility rate**: since September 2026 it has been **2.50 %**. Check the current figure at ecb.europa.eu, because it changes several times a year.
steps.key: When money gets more expensive, the future is worth less.
steps.tip: Try it: find the TLT long-bond ETF in Market and look at its 2022.

u18l4.title: The data that moves the market

texts: Good data, market in the red
Hugo
First Friday of the month. The US jobs figure is out.
Loads more jobs have been created than expected!
And the stock market… falls? I don't get it.
Why do you think it's falling?
The market fears rates will stay high
That's it. With so many jobs, the Fed is in less of a hurry to cut them.
The figure must be wrong
The figure is real. The market is thinking about what the Fed will do.
It's pure chance
There may be noise, but here there's a reason: interest rates.
The price already includes what's **expected**. What moves it is the **surprise**.
Good for the economy isn't always good for the stock market on the day.
Expected versus actual
The market expected one figure and got another. A **good** surprise, a **bad** one or **none** for the stock market?
Good
Bad
No surprise
Inflation expected at 3 %; comes in at 3.4 %
More inflation than expected: high rates for longer.
PMI expected at 49; comes in at 52
More activity than expected, and above 50: expansion.
GDP expected at +0.3 %; comes in at +0.3 %
It was already priced in: little to adjust.
GDP expected at +0.4 %; comes in at −0.1 %
The economy is doing worse than people thought.
Inflation expected at 2.9 %; comes in at 2.5 %
Less inflation than expected brings rate cuts closer.
The ECB cuts rates by 0.25 points, as expected
If everyone expected it, it was already priced in.
The Fed was expected to hold rates and raises them
Dearer money without warning: a bad surprise for the stock market.
Sort the seven figures.
The market doesn't react to whether a figure is good or bad, but to whether it's **better or worse than expected**. What's expected is already priced in.
Compare the figure with what was expected, not with last month.
Better, worse or as expected?

steps.title: The economic calendar
steps.body:
• **CPI/HICP:** inflation. It decides interest rates.
• **GDP:** how fast the economy is growing.
• **Jobs:** in the US, non-farm payrolls on the first Friday of each month; in Spain, the EPA (labour force survey) and registered unemployment.
• **PMI:** a monthly survey of purchasing managers. **Above 50 = expansion.** It comes out ahead of GDP.
• **Interest rate decisions** by the ECB and the Fed.
steps.key: The market doesn't react to whether the data is good or bad, but to whether it's better or worse than expected.
steps.tip: Try it: on the first Friday of the month, watch how the S&P 500 reacts in Market.

u18l5.title: Small and growth companies: what to look at

texts: «It's going to multiply by 10»
Marc
I've found a company whose sales grow 80 % every year.
On the forum they say it's going to multiply by 10!
Does it make money?
Not yet. It has €120m in cash and burns €10m a month.
What do you look at first?
How many months it can last and how it'll fund itself
Key point: 120 ÷ 10 = **12 months of cash**. After that, it'll have to raise money.
Nothing: if it's growing that fast, it'll be fine
Growing without cash is a race against the clock.
Its P/E
With no profit, the P/E is useless. Look at sales, margins and cash.
If it doesn't make money in time, it'll **raise capital**: your stake gets diluted.
Or it'll borrow. And with high interest rates, these companies suffer more.
No profits: what to look at?
A young company loses money while it grows. Is this a **good sign**, a **bad sign** or does it **tell you nothing**?
Good sign
Bad sign
Tells you nothing
Its sales grow strongly several years running
Sustained growth is the first thing you look for.
Gross margin of 70 %: each sale makes money
If each sale makes money, growing brings it closer to profit.
Cash for only 6 months
It will most likely need more money soon.
Lots of social media followers
Popularity doesn't pay salaries.
Raises capital every year
Every capital raise dilutes shareholders.
Cash for 30 months
Plenty of time to start making money.
On a forum they say «it's going to multiply by 10»
An opinion isn't data.
Its gross margin falls year after year
Each sale makes less: growing takes it further from profit.
Sort the eight clues.
With a loss-making company, the key question is **whether it will start making money before it runs out of cash**. Look at growth, gross margin and **months of cash = cash ÷ monthly burn**.
Does it bring it closer to profit or push it further away?
Sort each clue

steps.title: Many don't make it
steps.body:
• With no profit, the P/E is useless. You look at **price/sales**: market cap ÷ sales.
• Small companies can multiply… or disappear. More than half of US shares since 1926 returned less than Treasury bills.
• They're among the hardest hit when interest rates rise.
steps.key: With a loss-making company, the key question is whether it will start making money before it runs out of cash.
steps.tip: Try it: ask Lumi how to work out how many months of cash a company has.

texts: Inditex in 30 minutes
Laura
Laura analyses Inditex (2024 financial year) with a 10-question checklist. It's practice, **not a recommendation**.
Sales: €38,632m, up 7.5 %. Gross margin: 57.8 %. Profit: €5,866m, up 9 %.
Is it growing? Yes. Is it profitable? Very. Now: is it healthy? It has €11,495m in net cash.
What does that net cash tell you about its debt?
It has more cash than debt: very healthy
That's it. With net cash, that question answers itself.
That it owes €11,495m
**Net** cash is cash minus debt: it has money to spare.
You can't tell anything
You can: positive net cash means more cash than debt.
And it pays a €1.68 dividend. Now the hard one: is it expensive?
It counts as much as the others. A great business that's expensive can be a bad investment.
Red flags
The numbers sometimes warn you before the headlines do. **Good sign** or **red flag**?
Good sign
Red flag
Free cash flow is in line with profit
Profit is turning into real money.
Profit grows but cash doesn't
Where's the money? You need to ask.
Changes auditor and chief financial officer
Changes like that around the accounts call for explanations.
Constant capital raises
It doesn't generate the money it needs, and it dilutes you.
Has more cash than debt
It weathers any crisis better.
Pays the dividend with debt
A healthy dividend comes out of cash.
Executives sell lots of shares
The people who know it best are getting out.
Debt grows without profits growing
Borrowing more without earning more: a bad combination.
Sort the eight signs.
Red flags tend to be in **cash and debt**, not in the profit headline. If profit rises and cash doesn't, ask why.
Follow the money: is real cash coming in?
Sort each sign

steps.title: The 10-question checklist
steps.body:
1. Do I understand how it makes money?
2. Is it growing?
3. Is it profitable (margins, ROE, ROIC)?
4. Does it generate cash?
5. Is it financially healthy (debt)?
6. Does it have a moat?
7. Who runs it?
8. Is it expensive?
9. What could go wrong?
10. What would make me sell?
steps.key: If you can't explain in three sentences why you're buying a company, you're not ready to buy it yet.
steps.tip: Try it: pick a company in Market and go through the 10 questions with Lumi.

u18l1-1.prompt: Match each example with its moat.
options: A social network with billions of users
The management software a whole company uses
A drug company with a patented medicine
A big retailer that buys more cheaply than anyone else
The only oil pipeline in a region
u18l1-1.explanation: The five moats from Morningstar and Pat Dorsey.

u18l1-2.prompt: What moat does a payment system have when almost every shop accepts it and almost every customer uses it?
u18l1-2.explanation: The more shops accept it, the more customers want it, and vice versa.

u18l1-3.prompt: Which signs in the numbers suggest a moat? Tick all that apply.
u18l1-3.explanation: Constant losses point to exactly the opposite.

u18l1-4.prompt: Ana is analysing a trendy café with queues out the door that made a lot of money last year. Three similar ones have just opened 50 metres away. What does she conclude about its moat?
options: The moat depends on how the place is decorated
It has a huge moat: there are queues
Its moat is weak: it's easy to copy and people are already copying it
u18l1-4.explanation: If a business makes a lot of money and is easy to copy, competition will arrive.
feedback: Without an advantage that's hard to copy, there's no moat.
Being trendy isn't a moat: if it's easy to copy, competitors arrive and share out the queues.
Exactly: without something stopping others from doing the same, high profits attract competition.

u18l1-5.prompt: Bruno finds a company with a crystal-clear moat… trading on a P/E of 90 and growing at 10 % a year. What does he bear in mind?
options: That its PEG is 9: the price already assumes a huge amount
That with a moat like that, any price is fine
That a high P/E guarantees it will keep rising
u18l1-5.explanation: A good business also needs a good price.
feedback: Exactly: 90 ÷ 10 = 9. A great business can be a bad investment if you overpay.
Microsoft had a moat in 2000 too, and anyone who bought at the peak took about 16 years to break even.
It doesn't guarantee anything; it just signals very high expectations.

u18l2-2.prompt: Match each phase of the cycle with what usually happens.
u18l2-2.explanation: And then it starts all over again.
right: Rates go up and growth slows
Low rates and the economy starts to grow

u18l2-3.prompt: First week of September 2008: the US has just taken over Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac and there's talk of recession. What did the S&P 500 do in the following months?
u18l2-3.explanation: In the middle of the financial crisis, nobody knew how far the contagion to the real economy would spread. Cyclicals, like banks and industrials, were the most exposed.

u18l2-4.prompt: March 2009: unemployment is soaring and the headlines are terrible. The S&P 500 has fallen more than 50 % from its peak. What did it do next?
u18l2-4.explanation: With news that bad, almost nobody dared to make a decision. Remember that the stock market looks at what it expects months ahead, not at what's happening today.

options: A 10 % fall in the stock market
Two quarters in a row of falling GDP

u18l2-7.prompt: The data points to a slowdown. Pablo has almost his whole portfolio in banks, carmakers and hotels. What risk is he running?
options: He's heavily concentrated in cyclicals, which usually fall more if a recession comes
None: those sectors always go up
u18l2-7.explanation: Spreading across cyclical and defensive sectors makes you less dependent on the cycle.
feedback: Exactly: it's not about predicting the recession, but about not relying on a single kind of sector.
They do exist: food, healthcare, utilities…
They're precisely the most sensitive to the cycle: they fall more in recessions.

u18l2-9.prompt: Which sectors are defensive? Tick all that apply.

u18l3-2.prompt: Put in order what happens when the central bank raises rates.
u18l3-2.explanation: With a lag of 12 to 24 months between the first step and the last.

u18l3-3.prompt: The ECB raises rates by more than expected. Laura has a young tech company with no profits, a bank and a 30-year bond fund. Which part usually suffers least in the short term?
u18l3-3.explanation: Rate rises mainly punish whatever depends on the distant future.
feedback: It's the most sensitive: its value depends on profits a long way off.
It's one of the things that falls most when rates go up.
Exactly: at first, banks usually earn more on their loans. Though if the economy slows sharply, they suffer too.

u18l3-4.prompt: What is the ECB's inflation target?
u18l3-4.explanation: That's why it acts when inflation drifts away from 2 %.

u18l3-7.prompt: Match each concept with its meaning.
u18l3-7.explanation: As well as setting rates, central banks move the market by buying or offloading bonds.
right: What the ECB pays banks for lending it money
The central bank reduces the bonds it holds
The central bank buys bonds to inject money

u18l3-9.prompt: In 2022, tech shares and long-dated bonds fell at the same time.
u18l3-9.explanation: The Nasdaq fell more than 30 % and long-dated bonds more than 20 %: rising rates hit both.

u18l3-10.prompt: What do you reply to Lumi?
options: It has no effect at all
It's usually positive, but it depends on whether it was already expected and why they're cutting
u18l3-10.explanation: Cutting rates usually helps shares and bonds, but the surprise and the reason matter.
feedback: Interest rates are the price of money: they affect everything.
Ah! If they're cutting because a crisis is coming, maybe it's not such good news.
The opposite: it usually boosts the economy and helps shares and bonds… unless it's done out of fear of a crisis.
lines: The ECB has cut interest rates 📉
Is that good or bad for the stock market?

u18l4-1.prompt: Match each indicator with what it measures.
u18l4-1.explanation: The most closely watched data on the calendar.
right: Factory and services activity, by survey
How fast the economy is growing

u18l4-4.prompt: Inflation is expected at 2.8 % and comes in at 3.3 %. You have a big position in long-dated bonds. What's most likely to happen that day?
options: The bonds fall: the market now expects higher rates
u18l4-4.explanation: What counts is the gap between the figure and what was expected.
feedback: 2.8 % was expected, not 3.3 %: there's a surprise.
Exactly: an upside surprise in inflation puts pressure on bond prices.
A worse-than-expected figure pushes rate cuts further away: they would normally fall.

u18l4-6.prompt: Why is the PMI followed so closely?
options: Because it measures the price of gold
Because it comes out ahead of GDP
Because the stock exchange publishes it
u18l4-6.explanation: It's a monthly survey that arrives long before the GDP figure.

u18l4-9.prompt: Which data usually moves markets most? Tick all that apply.
options: The number of visitors to a museum
Interest rate decisions by the ECB and the Fed
u18l4-9.explanation: Rates, inflation and jobs shape monetary policy.

u18l4-10.prompt: GDP was expected at +0.3 % and comes in at +0.3 %. Most likely reaction?
options: Not much: it was already priced in
u18l4-10.explanation: Without a surprise, there's not much to adjust.

u18l5-6.prompt: A company keeps selling more, but its gross margin is 5 % and falling: almost everything it takes in goes on the cost of making the sale. How does it look?
options: Bad sign: growing like this doesn't bring it any closer to making money
The margin doesn't matter if sales are going up
u18l5-6.explanation: Look at whether each sale makes money, not just how many sales there are.
feedback: Growing by selling at almost no margin doesn't bring profits closer: it pushes them further away.
Exactly: growth is only worth it if each sale leaves something behind.
The margin tells you whether growth creates value or eats it up.

u18l5-7.prompt: Why is the P/E no use for a company that's losing money?
options: Because without earnings it comes out negative and makes no sense
Because it's forbidden to calculate it
Because it always comes out at 15
u18l5-7.explanation: That's why you look at sales, margins and cash.

u18l5-11.prompt: A young company that still loses money: good or bad sign?
options: It spends more on ads than it sells
It needs a capital increase every year
Its gross margin falls every year
Its customers come back and pay every month
It has cash left for two and a half years
u18l5-11.explanation: The good signs bring it closer to making money before it runs out of cash. The bad ones push it further away or force it to raise money, which usually dilutes you.

u18l5-12.prompt: You own shares in a young company that loses money. It announces a capital increase: it will issue lots of new shares and you won't buy any. What happens to your share of the company?
options: It grows: new money comes into the company
It gets smaller: the cake is shared among more shares
It doesn't change: I still have the same shares
u18l5-12.explanation: If there are more shares and you don't buy, your percentage falls: that's dilution. It's very common in companies that burn cash, which is why you look at months of cash.
feedback: Money comes into the company, but your slice of the cake shrinks.
That's dilution: you have the same shares, but out of a bigger total.
You have the same ones, but now there are more in total: your percentage falls.

u18l5-13.prompt: Two made-up companies with no profits sell €100m a year. One is worth €300m on the stock market; the other, €3,000m. Which is more expensive by price/sales?
options: The €3,000m one: you pay 30 times its sales
Both the same: they sell the same
u18l5-13.explanation: With no profits, you compare what it's worth with what it sells: 3 times sales versus 30. The expensive one needs to grow enormously to justify its price.

u18l5-14.prompt: What do you reply to Lumi?
options: With the P/E, like all of them
With its sales, its gross margin and its months of cash
u18l5-14.explanation: With no profit, the P/E is no use. You look at how much you pay for its sales, whether each sale makes money (gross margin) and how long its cash will last.
feedback: Popularity doesn't pay salaries.
With no profit, the P/E comes out negative and tells you nothing.
Of course: price/sales, margin and cash. The P/E is no use here.
lines: This company sells 80 % more every year.
But it loses money! How do I value it without a P/E?

u18l6-1.prompt: Put the first five steps of the checklist in order.
options: Do I understand how it makes money?
u18l6-1.explanation: First understand the business; then its numbers.

u18l6-8.prompt: You've run the checklist on a company: it's growing, very profitable, generates cash, has no debt and has a strong brand. But it trades on a P/E well above its historical average. What do you conclude?
options: A safe buy: it's a great business
It's a great business, but I need to decide whether the price leaves a margin of safety
u18l6-8.explanation: A good business also needs a good price.
feedback: A great business isn't the same as a great investment: the price matters.
Nothing suggests that: it's a healthy business at a demanding price.
Exactly: question 8 («is it expensive?») carries as much weight as the others.

u18l6-10.prompt: What should a good investment thesis include? Tick everything that applies.
options: Why the price is below the value
u18l6-10.explanation: A thesis explains why the business is worth more than its price, and when you'd stop believing it.

u18l6-11.prompt: You apply the checklist to two made-up companies in the same sector, at the same P/E. A grows, generates cash and has more cash than debt. B grows just as much, but its profit doesn't reach its cash and it raises capital every year. Which passes the test better?
options: Both the same: they have the same P/E
A: it grows, turns profit into cash and is healthy
B: it grows just as much
u18l6-11.explanation: At the same price, the winner is the one that answers «does it generate cash?» and «is it healthy?» better. The red flags are usually in cash and debt, not in the profit headline.
feedback: The P/E is the same; the quality of the profit isn't.
That's it: at the same price, the one that generates cash and doesn't dilute you is the better buy.
It grows on paper, but doesn't generate cash and dilutes you every year.

u18l6-13.prompt: Is it data for your analysis or is it noise?
options: A message saying the share «is going to explode»
Sales over the last five years
Its debt compared with what it earns
u18l6-13.explanation: An analysis is built on the business and its accounts; what the price did this week or what people say on social media doesn't count.
